title.zh: 云中城堡与羊毛云吊桥
title.en: The Cloud-Castle with the Wool-Cloud Drawbridge

content:
从前呀，在一个天空总是软软的、空气尝起来像温热的牛奶加蜂蜜的地方，住着一位叫艾拉拉的小姑娘。她穿着蒲公英绒毛编成的小拖鞋，睡裙是用暮色蓝的丝绸缝的。她的头发卷卷的，像刚醒来的蕨类小叶子；眼睛亮亮的，像萤火虫快要落在叶子上时，那一点点安静又温柔的光。

艾拉拉住在“低语草甸”的最边上，一座小木屋里。那里，每根小草都会在风儿轻轻路过时，哼起低低的摇篮曲；瓢虫会停在你的鼻尖上，就为了轻轻说一句“你好呀”。

每天傍晚，当太阳慢慢滑到天鹅绒山丘后面，把云朵染成蜜桃粉和淡紫灰的时候，艾拉拉就会爬上窗台，把光脚丫轻轻收在身子底下，静静看着天空一点点、一点点地变样子——像一块慢慢融化的糖。

而每天晚上——从不例外——她都能看见它：云朵城堡。

它飘在最高的山丘上方，不高不低，不挨着天，也不碰着地，就那么安安静静地待在那儿，轻得像一声叹息。它的塔楼是糖丝雾气绕成的，塔尖顶着银色的星光，从不眨眼睛，只悄悄地、柔柔地闪呀闪。城墙是珍珠白的，总在轻轻变化，像凉凉的玻璃窗上呵出的一口气。而城堡那扇宽宽的、敞开的大门——宽得能让三道月光并排手牵手走进去——上面挂着一座羊毛云吊桥。

啊，羊毛云吊桥！它可不是木头做的，也不是绳子，更不是彩虹。它全是由云朵羊毛织成的——厚厚、蓬蓬、软得像一朵被午后阳光暖透的蒲公英伞。傍晚时分，它就轻轻垂在空气里，微微晃呀晃，像两棵正在做梦的树之间，挂起的一张小吊床。艾拉拉已经看了好多好多晚，可那座吊桥，一次也没放下来过。

直到今晚。

今晚的空气格外香甜——像刚出炉的苹果派，还混着揉碎的薄荷叶。小草也换了一支新曲子：慢悠悠、圆润润、沉甸甸的，像水壶快睡着前，最后唱出的那一声咕噜。

艾拉拉眨了眨眼。咦？羊毛云吊桥……真的在往下放！

不是一下子“哗啦”掉下来，也没有“吱呀呀”的响声。而是慢慢地——噢，真真是慢得让人心都化开了——像一只猫咪伸完长长的懒腰后，心满意足地舒展身体。天空里飘下一声轻轻的“呼——”，像羽毛无声地飘落。云朵羊毛缓缓松开，一点一点垂下来，拖着小小的、毛茸茸的云絮，像蒲公英的小伞兵。它先轻轻碰了碰最高的草尖，再轻轻蹭了蹭艾拉拉小屋旁青苔斑斑的石头墙，最后，发出一声像叹息变成微笑那样的声音：“噗——嗯”，软软地、稳稳地，落在地上，就像一个枕头，轻轻落进被窝里。

艾拉拉没有跑，也没有喊。她只是轻轻滑下窗台，踮起脚尖，踩过地板（地板在蒲公英拖鞋底下，也轻轻叹了口气），双手推开小木门，走了出去。

小草凉凉的、软软的，摸起来特别舒服。头顶的星星一颗接一颗地眨眼睛——不急不快，慢悠悠的，像眼皮沉沉的、快要坠入梦乡的样子。而羊毛云吊桥呢，正泛着淡淡的光，里头透出来的光不亮，却特别暖，像一支裹着棉布的蜡烛，心里暖烘烘的。

艾拉拉抬起小脚，轻轻踏上了吊桥。

哎呀——是什么感觉呀！

比鹅毛还软，比草地上的小蘑菇还弹。脚底下的云朵微微托起她一下，又温柔地稳稳托住。她又迈了一步，再一步。每走一步，吊桥就像在跟着她呼吸——一起轻轻抬起来，再轻轻落下去，像熟睡中起伏的小胸口。还有些小星星点点的光，比雀斑还小，从羊毛里悠悠浮上来，绕着她的手腕、脚踝转圈圈，痒痒的，逗得她忍不住笑出声——轻轻的、闷闷的笑声，像温热的茶水里，咕嘟咕嘟冒上来的泡泡。

吊桥上没有台阶，只有这一条路，宽宽的、暖暖的、欢迎你来的路，弯弯地向上延伸，像一个困倦的小画家，随手画出来的小径。艾拉拉走着走着，四周越来越安静——不是空空的静，而是满满的、在认真听你说话的静。连蟋蟀都停下了“唧唧唧”，连微风都收起了翅膀，轻轻歇在一朵毛茛花上。

走到一半时，她看见它们啦：云朵小羊。

它们不像地球上的羊那样又大又壮、毛又厚。它们小小的，大概就茶杯那么大，身子像打发好的蛋白霜，蹄子踩在地上，留下一个个小小、淡淡、像逗号一样的脚印。眼睛黑黑亮亮的，温和又亲切，像被河水洗得圆润润的鹅卵石；身上的羊毛，也闪着和吊桥一模一样的、软软的光。

其中一只小羊，比别的更小一点，额头上还打着一个问号似的卷卷，轻轻往前走了一步。它没“咩——”地叫，而是“嗡——”地哼了一声——一个清清亮亮、低低圆圆、暖暖的音符，像傍晚最后一声风铃，在暮色里轻轻荡开。

艾拉拉就坐在了羊毛云铺成的小路上，盘着腿。那只小羊哒哒地走过来，把毛茸茸的小脑袋，靠在她的膝盖上。它的羊毛暖暖的、干干的，闻起来像晒过太阳的干净床单。艾拉拉轻轻摸了它一下——就一下——小羊的哼声变得更深了，轻轻震动着，从她的指尖，顺着胳膊，一直传到肩膀，最后像一枚小小的、呼噜呼噜的小月亮，安安静静地停在那里。

更多的云朵小羊飘了过来，不挤也不推，只是松松地、软软地围成一个圈。一只躺在她左脚边，一只把下巴搁在她腿上，还有一只，把尾巴轻轻绕在她手腕上，像一圈雾气做的手镯。它们不说话，也不需要说话。它们的安静，就是最温柔的话：*你很安全。你被欢迎。你就这样，刚刚好，属于这里。*

忽然，从高高的天上——不是从城堡里，而是从城堡后头的天空里——传来一阵声音：“叮——咚……叮——咚……”是水滴落入池子里的声音。不是下雨，也不是瀑布，就是安静、稳稳的水滴——一滴……两滴……三滴……每滴落下来，都发出轻轻的“叮”一声，像一只小小的银铃，在耳边轻轻回响。

艾拉拉抬起头。

就在吊桥尽头的前方，城堡的大门敞开着——像打了个大大的哈欠，拱形的门边镶着发光的珍珠，和吊桥一样，泛着暖暖的光。透过门，她看见一个院子，铺着光滑、浅浅的石头——每块石头上都有细细弯弯的纹路，像风儿留下的指纹。院子正中央，立着一棵树——不高，也不茂密，细细的、柔柔的，树枝光秃秃的，却亮着柔和的金光，像玻璃罩里的烛火。

树下坐着一个人。

不大，也不高大，只是安安静静地坐着——不急不躁，不紧不慢——坐在一把云朵木刻成的小凳子上，凳子光滑、洁白，像白桦树皮。他穿着一件袍子，颜色是星星还没出来前的那抹暮色蓝，里面细细地织着银线和最柔软的金线。头发是雪一样的白，却暖得像刚烤好的面包。他双手捧着一个小东西，圆圆的、亮亮的、柔柔地闪着光——像一道被轻轻捉住的月光，裹在丝绒里。

他没有马上抬头。

他在等。

艾拉拉也等着。

她看着光在院子里的石头上轻轻流动；她感受着云朵小羊靠着她的那份温暖；她听着远处屋顶上，雨滴敲打的“叮——咚……叮——咚……”声——轻得像妈妈哼摇篮曲时，用木勺轻轻敲着温热的杯子。

然后——一声深深的、长长的叹息，像风儿走了很久的路，终于轻轻落了下来。

羊毛云吊桥没有“啪嗒”掉下来，而是像一朵花，轻轻“舒展开”了。

像蒲公英吹散种子时，那一团绒毛在阳光里缓缓散开，吊桥的边缘变得柔和，轻轻消融，让光透进来——不刺眼，不耀眼，是金灿灿、蜜糖般浓稠的光，像温热的糖浆，悄悄漫过艾拉拉光光的脚趾。

云朵小羊用脑袋轻轻顶了顶她的手。艾拉拉低头一看，发现它羊毛上，细细地闪着银色的丝线——不是电线，也不是绳子，而是“悄悄话”，由安静的愿望、半梦半醒的梦，一丝一丝纺成的。

然后——她听见了。

不是用耳朵听的，更像是在胸口里，在心跳旁边，轻轻响起的。

一个声音。不响亮，也不命令谁。只是……存在在那里。像夏日午后蜂巢的嗡嗡声，或者雪要落下前，世界屏住呼吸的那一秒。

*你不用第一个跨过去，* 那声音轻轻说——不是用字，而是用感觉告诉她的。*你只要相信，这座桥是真的，就足够了。*

艾拉拉眨眨眼。她什么也没大声说出来，甚至自己都没想过这么清楚的句子。可那个声音，知道。

她看了看皮普和皮帕。他们手拉着手，站得笔直，眼睛睁得圆圆的——不是害怕，而是满心满眼的惊奇，像两个孩子，看萤火虫一颗接一颗飞进玻璃罐子里。他们的呼吸也一模一样：吸……呼……吸……呼……像小小的潮水，一遍遍抚平岸边的鹅卵石。

艾拉拉向前迈了一小步。

院子里的石头，暖暖地托住了她的脚心——不烫，不凉，就是刚刚好，像清晨沾着露水的苔藓，被太阳晒得暖烘烘的。地面轻轻“嘘——”了一声，好像石头们也在深深呼出一口气，欢迎她来。

她又迈出一步。

羊毛云吊桥微微闪动——不是雾气散开，而是像一层轻纱，轻轻向两边拉开，露出后面一直静静等候的东西。就在那层云光的后面，站着三个身影。

不是巨人，不是国王，甚至……不太像大人。

他们够得着城堡最低的窗户，但肩膀圆圆的，头发打着温柔的卷儿，像刚出炉的肉桂卷；袍子是暮色蓝的布做的，上面绣着一闪一闪的小星星——艾拉拉还注意到，是用手一针一线绣的，因为其中一只袖子上，有一根线头松松的，旁边那颗小星星，还微微晃了一下，像一只快睡着的眼睛。

他们是云朵城堡的守护者。

最高的那位守护者笑了——不是咧开嘴，而是眼角漾开温柔的细纹，琥珀色的眼睛亮亮的。“我们一直在等你的脚步声呢。”她说，声音像海螺做成的风铃，叮叮当当。

“城堡不会为王冠或钥匙打开，”第二位守护者说，声音更深些，像溪水缓缓流过光滑的石头。他伸出一只手——不是要握手，而是摊开掌心，一只小小的、空心的橡果杯里，盛着一团光，像被轻轻捧住的月光。“它只为安静打开，为倾听打开，为你来了——哪怕膝盖有点抖，也依然来了——而打开。”

第三位守护者最小，她走上前，慢慢、轻轻地跪下来，直到眼睛和艾拉拉一样高。她的头发香香的，像干草上刚落下的雨，又像烤得暖暖的面包。“最重要的是，”她轻轻地说，“它只为那种不求回报的善良而打开。”

艾拉拉低下头，看看还靠着她小腿的云朵小羊。它的羊毛一鼓一鼓的，软软的，稳稳的，像一颗裹在毛绒里的小心跳。

她伸下手——不是把它推开，也不是赶它走——只是把手心，轻轻地、平平地，贴在它暖暖的、毛绒绒的身上。

小羊长长地、深深地，叹了一口气。

那是一声满足极了、幸福极了的叹息——就在这一瞬间，它的羊毛开始发光了！不刺眼，只是暖暖的——像夜里炉膛里，盖着灰烬的余火。一根根细细的银线，从羊毛里轻轻升起，像蒲公英的小伞，悠悠地、转着圈儿往上飘，飘到吊桥的底下，然后——“缝”了起来。

不是用针，也不是用线。

是用温柔。

是用耐心。

是用一种静静的、笃定的信念：有些东西，从来不是靠力气绑在一起的，而是靠心意，一点一点，轻轻系牢的。

吊桥没有放下，它开花了。

像黎明时分，花朵慢慢绽放，一片片云朵花瓣，软软的、蓬蓬的，边缘泛着淡淡的紫罗兰光，一层一层，轻轻舒展开。而在花瓣之下，一条小路出现了。不是石头铺的，不是木头搭的，甚至……也不是云朵。

它是用一个个“时刻”织成的：故事开始前那一秒的屏息……把心爱的小被子拉到下巴边的重量……黑暗里，爸爸妈妈均匀、安稳的呼吸声……被抱着回家睡觉时，脸颊贴着软软毛衣的感觉，整个世界都模糊了，却无比安心。

皮普深深吸了口气。皮帕紧紧握了握他的手。他们一起，踏上了这条路。

没有雷声，没有欢呼。只有一声轻轻的“唰——唰——”，像小拖鞋踩在地毯上。然后，他们就并肩走着，朝三位守护者走去。守护者们微微低下了头——不是深深鞠躬，只是刚好那么一点点，像在说：*我们看见你了。真高兴，你来了。*

艾拉拉跟在后面。

云朵小羊一直陪在她身边，那份暖意，是她稳稳的依靠。

他们走着走着，院子也悄悄变了——不是一下子，而是像翻一本心爱的旧书那样，一页一页，温柔地翻过。石头渐渐软成了厚厚的苔藓。空气更甜了，飘着烤苹果和洋甘菊茶的香气。还有些小光点，比萤火虫的肚子还小，像流星一样轻轻飘落——落在皮普的肩膀上，皮帕的头发上，艾拉拉的手腕上——每一颗都轻轻闪一下，像一个暖暖的吻，然后化作一阵酥酥麻麻的暖意。

院子中央，有一张矮矮的圆桌子，是白桦木做的，表面光滑，摸起来暖暖的。桌上放着三只小杯子——结实、小巧，把手弯弯的，像小羊的角；还有一只大壶，里面装着会流动的液体，颜色温柔得没法叫出名字：玫瑰金、天空银、暮色紫。

最高的守护者倒起水来。

不多，不少。

刚刚好。

艾拉拉双手捧起自己的杯子。杯子暖暖的——不烫，就像把一只刚睡着的小鸟，轻轻捧在手心里。她喝了一口。

味道像“安全”。

像被人轻轻掖好被角。

像夜深人静、你已半梦半醒时，有人在你耳边，轻轻说一句：“我爱你。”

皮普和皮帕坐在像压扁的云朵一样的垫子上——软软的，弹弹的，闻起来有香草和雨的味道。他们也喝了一口。皮普的眼睛闭了整整三秒钟。皮帕长长地、慢慢地叹了口气，肩膀一下子松了下来，仿佛已经举着它们，许多年了。

守护者们没再说话。他们只是静静地坐在那里——不着急，不催促，散发着一种让钟表都忘记嘀嗒的安宁。

艾拉拉看着皮普的眼皮越来越沉。看着皮帕的手指慢慢松开杯子，让它安稳地躺在她怀里。看着云朵小羊蜷成一个毛茸茸的、弯弯的月牙，乖乖卧在她脚边——呼吸深深、缓缓，身上的光也变得均匀、柔和，像一盏盖着薄纱的灯笼。

守护者们轻轻站了起来——安静地……
contentEn:
Once upon a time, in a land where the sky was always soft and the air tasted like warm milk and honey, there lived a little girl named Elara who wore slippers made of woven dandelion fluff and a nightgown stitched from twilight-blue silk. Her hair curled like sleepy ferns, and her eyes held the quiet glow of fireflies just before they settle on a leaf.

Elara lived in a cottage at the very edge of the Meadow of Whispering Grass — a place where blades of grass hummed low, lullaby notes when the wind passed by, and ladybugs paused on your nose just to say hello. Every evening, as the sun sank behind the Velvet Hills, painting the clouds peach-pink and lavender-grey, Elara would climb onto her windowsill, tuck her bare feet beneath her, and watch the sky begin its slow, sweet change.

And every evening — without fail — she saw it: the Cloud-Castle.

It floated high above the tallest hill, not quite touching the sky, not quite resting on the earth — just *there*, gentle as a sigh. Its towers were spun from spun-sugar mist, its turrets tipped with silver starlight that never blinked, only shimmered. Its walls were pearly-white and ever-shifting, like breath on a cool windowpane. And across its wide, open gate — wide enough for three moonbeams to stroll through side-by-side — hung the Wool-Cloud Drawbridge.

Ah, the Wool-Cloud Drawbridge! It wasn’t wood or rope or even rainbows. It was made entirely of cloud-wool — thick, fluffy, pillowy soft, like the inside of a dandelion clock stretched wide and warmed by afternoon sun. It hung low in the evening air, swaying just a little, like a hammock strung between two dreaming trees. And though Elara had watched it for many, many nights, the drawbridge had never once lowered.

Not until tonight.

Tonight, the air smelled especially sweet — like baked apples and crushed mint — and the grass hummed a new tune: slow, round, and deep, like a kettle singing just before it sleeps. Elara blinked. The Wool-Cloud Drawbridge… was *lowering*.

Not all at once. Not with a creak or a groan. But slowly — oh, so slowly — like a cat stretching after a long nap. A soft *whoosh* whispered down from the sky, like feathers falling in silence. The wool-cloud unspooled, drifting lower and lower, trailing tiny puffs like dandelion seeds. It touched the very tips of the tallest grasses — then the mossy stone wall beside Elara’s cottage — and finally, with a sound like a sigh turning into a smile, it settled gently onto the ground with a soft *poomph*, like a pillow landing on a bed.

Elara didn’t run. She didn’t shout. She simply slipped off the windowsill, tiptoed across the floorboards (which sighed softly under her dandelion slippers), opened the cottage door with both hands, and stepped outside.

The grass felt cool and kind beneath her toes. The stars above blinked one by one — not fast, but slow, like eyelids heavy with dreams. And the Wool-Cloud Drawbridge glowed faintly, lit from within by a light that wasn’t bright, but *warm*, like the heart of a candle wrapped in cotton.

Elara took one small step onto it.

And oh — what a feeling!

It was softer than goose-down. Springier than a meadow mushroom. It rose up just a little under her foot, then settled, holding her steady. She took another step. Then another. With each step, the drawbridge seemed to breathe with her — rising, falling, rising, falling — like a sleeping chest. Tiny sparkles, no bigger than freckles, floated up from the wool and danced around her wrists and ankles, tickling just enough to make her giggle — a soft, hushed giggle, like bubbles rising in warm tea.

No stairs led up to the castle — only the drawbridge itself, wide and welcoming, curling gently upward like a path drawn by a sleepy artist. As Elara walked, the air grew quieter, not empty, but full of *listening*. Even the crickets paused mid-chirp. Even the breeze folded its wings and rested on a buttercup.

Halfway up, she saw them: the Cloud-Sheep.

They weren’t big or loud or woolly like Earth-sheep. They were small — about the size of teacups — with bodies like spun meringue and hooves that left tiny, fading prints shaped like commas. Their eyes were dark, shiny, and kind — like polished river stones — and their fleece shimmered with the same soft light as the drawbridge.

One sheep, smaller than the rest, with a curl on its forehead like a question mark, stepped forward. It didn’t bleat. It *hummed* — a single, clear note, low and round and warm, like the last chime of a wind-bell at dusk.

Elara sat down right there on the wool-cloud path, cross-legged, and the little sheep padded over and leaned its head against her knee. Its wool was warm and dry and smelled like sunshine on clean linen. She stroked it once — just once — and its hum deepened, vibrating gently through her fingers and up her arm, all the way to her shoulder, where it settled like a tiny, purring moon.

More Cloud-Sheep drifted near, not crowding, not pushing — just gathering in a loose, soft circle. One lay down beside her left foot. Another rested its chin on her lap. A third curled its tail around her wrist like a bracelet of mist. They didn’t speak. They didn’t need to. Their stillness spoke for them: *You are safe. You are welcome. You belong here, just as you are.*

From somewhere high above — not from the castle, but from the sky *behind* it — came a sound: the gentle *plink-plonk* of water droplets falling into a pool. Not rain. Not a waterfall. Just quiet, steady drops — one… two… three… — each landing with a soft *ping* that echoed like a tiny silver bell.

Elara lifted her eyes.

There, just beyond the drawbridge’s end, stood the castle gate — wide open, arched like a yawn, lined with pearls that glowed with the same warm light. Through it, she could see a courtyard paved with smooth, pale stones — each stone patterned with faint, swirling lines, like fingerprints of the wind. In the center of the courtyard stood a single tree — not tall, not leafy, but slender and graceful — its branches bare, yet glowing with soft, golden light, like candle-flames caught in glass.

And beneath the tree sat a figure.

Not large. Not towering. Just sitting — calmly, patiently — on a stool carved from cloud-wood, smooth and pale as birch bark. The figure wore a robe the colour of twilight just before stars appear — deep blue, shot through with threads of silver and softest gold. Their hair fell in loose waves, white as fresh snow, but warm as toast. And in their hands, they held something small and round and softly gleaming — like a captured moonbeam wrapped in silk.

They did not look up right away.

They waited.

Elara waited too.

She watched the light ripple across the courtyard stones. She felt the gentle weight of the Cloud-Sheep leaning against her. She heard the *plink-plonk* of the distant

plink-plonk of the distant rain-drum on the castle roof—soft as lullaby fingers tapping a wooden spoon against a warm mug.

Then—a sigh, deep and slow, like wind settling after a long journey.

The wool-cloud drawbridge didn’t *drop*. It *unfurled*.

Like a dandelion puff releasing its seeds into a sunlit breeze, the bridge softened at the edges, dissolving just enough to let light through—not sharp or bright, but golden and honey-thick, pooling around Elara’s bare toes like warm syrup. The Cloud-Sheep nudged her hand, and when she looked down, she saw tiny silver threads shimmering along its fleece—not wires or strings, but *whispers*, spun from quiet wishes and half-remembered dreams.

And then—she heard it.

Not with her ears, exactly. More like behind her ribs.

A voice. Not loud. Not commanding. Just… present. Like the hum of a beehive on a summer afternoon, or the hush right before snow begins to fall.

*You don’t need to cross first,* it whispered—not in words, but in feeling. *You only need to believe the bridge is real.*

Elara blinked. She hadn’t said anything aloud. She hadn’t even thought the words quite that way. Yet the voice knew.

She glanced at Pip and Pippa. They stood side by side, hands clasped tight, eyes wide—not with fear, but wonder, like children watching fireflies gather in a jar. Their breaths matched: in… out… in… out… like little tides smoothing pebbles on a shore.

Elara took one small step forward.

The courtyard stones warmed beneath her feet—not hot, not cold—just *right*, like sun-warmed moss after morning dew. A soft *shush* rose from the ground, as if the stones themselves were sighing in welcome.

She took another step.

The wool-cloud drawbridge shimmered—not like mist vanishing, but like a curtain parting to reveal something that had been there all along, waiting patiently. And there, just beyond the veil of cloud-light, stood three figures.

Not giants. Not kings. Not even grown-ups, exactly.

They were tall enough to reach the castle’s lowest windows, but their shoulders rounded softly, their hair floated in gentle spirals like cinnamon rolls fresh from the oven, and their robes were stitched from twilight-blue cloth embroidered with tiny, blinking stars—stitched *by hand*, Elara noticed, because one sleeve had a loose thread, and the star beside it wobbled ever so slightly, like a sleepy eye.

They were the Keepers of the Cloud-Castle.

The tallest Keeper smiled—not with teeth, but with crinkles around kind, amber eyes. “We’ve been expecting your footsteps,” she said, and her voice sounded like wind chimes made of seashells.

“The castle doesn’t open for crowns or keys,” added the second Keeper, whose voice was deeper, like water moving over smooth stones. He held out a hand—not to shake, but to show a small, hollow acorn cup, filled with something that glowed like captured moonlight. “It opens for stillness. For listening. For showing up, even when your knees feel wobbly.”

The third Keeper, smallest of all, stepped forward and knelt—gently, slowly—until her eyes were level with Elara’s. Her hair smelled like rain on dry grass and warm bread. “Most of all,” she whispered, “it opens for kindness that doesn’t ask for anything back.”

Elara looked down at the Cloud-Sheep, still leaning against her leg. Its fleece pulsed, soft and steady, like a heartbeat wrapped in fluff.

She reached down—not to push it away, not to shoo it off—but to rest her palm flat against its warm, woolly side.

And the sheep *sighed*.

A long, slow, deeply contented sigh—and as it did, its fleece began to *glow*. Not brightly, but warmly—like embers banked for the night. One by one, tiny silver threads lifted from its fleece, rising like dandelion clocks, weaving upward in lazy spirals until they met the underside of the drawbridge—and *stitched*.

Not with needle or thread.

With *tenderness*.

With *patience*.

With the quiet certainty that some things are held together not by force, but by care.

The drawbridge didn’t lower. It *bloomed*.

Like a flower opening at dawn, layers of cloud-petal unfurled—soft, pillowy, edged with faint lavender light—and beneath them, a path appeared. Not stone. Not wood. Not even cloud.

It was woven from *moments*: the hush before a story begins… the weight of a favorite blanket pulled up to the chin… the sound of a parent’s breath, slow and steady, in the dark… the memory of being carried home asleep, cheek pressed to a soft sweater, world blurred and safe.

Pip took a breath. Pippa squeezed his hand. Together, they stepped onto the path.

No thunder. No fanfare. Just a soft *hush-shush*—like slippers on carpet—and then they were walking, side by side, toward the Keepers, who bowed their heads—not low, but just enough to say, *We see you. We’re glad you’re here.*

Elara followed.

The Cloud-Sheep stayed beside her, its warmth a steady anchor.

As they walked, the courtyard changed—not all at once, but gently, like pages turning in a well-loved book. The stones softened into tufts of moss. The air grew sweeter, carrying the scent of baked apples and chamomile tea. Tiny lights, no bigger than firefly bellies, drifted down like falling stars—landing softly on Pip’s shoulder, Pippa’s hair, Elara’s wrist—each one pulsing once, softly, before dissolving into a warm tingle.

At the heart of the courtyard stood a low, round table carved from birchwood, its surface smooth and warm to the touch. On it rested three mugs—small, sturdy, with handles shaped like curled sheep’s horns—and a pitcher filled with liquid that swirled with colors too soft to name: rose-gold, sky-silver, dusk-lavender.

The tallest Keeper poured.

Not too much. Not too little.

Just enough.

Elara cradled her mug. It was warm—not hot—like holding a sleeping bird in your palms. She sipped.

It tasted like safety.

Like being tucked in.

Like hearing *“I love you”* whispered just once, late at night, when you’re already half-dreaming.

Pip and Pippa sat on cushions shaped like flattened clouds—soft, springy, smelling faintly of vanilla and rain. They sipped too. Pip’s eyes closed for three whole seconds. Pippa sighed, long and slow, and her shoulders dropped, as if she’d been holding them up for years.

The Keepers didn’t speak again. They simply *were*—present, unhurried, radiating the kind of calm that makes clocks forget to tick.

Elara watched Pip’s eyelids grow heavy. Watched Pippa’s fingers loosen their grip on her mug, letting it rest safely in her lap. Watched the Cloud-Sheep curl itself into a soft, woolly crescent at her feet—its breathing deep and slow, its fleece now glowing with a soft, even light, like a lantern covered with gauze.
